why: Risk assessment is the core of every GRC job and the first thing interviews test: give a candidate a scenario and see whether they can turn it into a clear risk, score it with a method, propose a treatment and explain it to a manager. The same skills cover suppliers and business continuity, two areas that NIS2 and DORA have made mandatory.
outcome: write precise risk statements, build likelihood and impact scales, score inherent and residual risk, run an assessment with ISO 27005 or EBIOS Risk Manager, quantify a risk in money (SLE, ARO, ALE) and compare it with a control’s cost, choose and document a treatment, keep a risk register, assess suppliers and set RTO and RPO with a business impact analysis.

lessons.title: The risk management process
text: A risk is the effect of uncertainty on objectives: something that may or may not happen and would affect what the organisation is trying to achieve. In information security, a risk is usually described as a scenario: a threat exploits a vulnerability on an asset and causes an impact. Risk management does not try to remove every risk, which is impossible; it tries to know the main risks and keep them at a level management accepts.

ISO 31000, the general standard for risk management, describes a process that ISO 27005 applies to information security. First, establish the context: scope, objectives, stakeholders, criteria and scales. Then the risk assessment, in three steps: identification (what could happen), analysis (how likely, how serious) and evaluation (compare with the acceptance criteria and rank). Then treatment: decide what to do and plan it. Throughout, monitoring and review, and communication with the people concerned. The process is a cycle, repeated at least once a year and after any major change.

Two levels of risk are compared. Inherent (or gross) risk is the level before taking existing controls into account, or with none. Residual (or net) risk is the level that remains with the controls in place. The difference shows the value of the controls, and residual risk is what management must accept or treat further.

Every risk has a risk owner: the manager who has the authority and the budget to decide on its treatment, usually on the business side. The GRC analyst facilitates the assessment, challenges the scores and follows the actions, but does not own the risks. When a risk owner accepts a risk, the decision is recorded with their name and a date.

Risk appetite is the amount of risk the organisation is willing to pursue or keep to reach its objectives, set by management in general terms. Risk tolerance turns it into limits per area, for example “no residual risk above 9 on a 16-point scale for customer data”. Risk capacity is the maximum the organisation could absorb before failing. Keep these terms distinct: interviewers like to check them.
points: Risk = a threat exploiting a vulnerability on an asset, with an impact; described as a scenario.
ISO 31000 / ISO 27005: context → identification → analysis → evaluation → treatment, with monitoring and communication throughout.
Inherent risk: before controls. Residual risk: with controls in place.
The risk owner is a manager with authority and budget; the GRC analyst facilitates and follows up.
Appetite (what we are willing to take), tolerance (limits per area), capacity (what we could survive).

example.code:
Context      Scope: online shop and customer data. Scales: likelihood 1-4, impact 1-4.
Identify     Ransomware encrypts the shop servers and backups
Analyse      Likelihood 3 (possible this year), impact 4 (shop down > 1 week)
Evaluate     Inherent 12 / 16, above the tolerance of 8 -> must be treated
Treat        Offline backups + restore tests + EDR on servers
Residual     Likelihood 2, impact 3 -> 6 / 16, accepted by the e-commerce director
Monitor      KRI: last successful restore test < 90 days
example.note: One risk taken through the whole cycle, from context to monitoring.

lessons.title: Writing risks and building scales
text: A badly written risk cannot be assessed. “Cyber attack” or “GDPR” are topics, not risks. A good risk statement has a cause, an event and a consequence: “Because remote access to the ERP uses passwords only (cause), an attacker could take over an employee account through phishing (event), leading to the theft of customer data, a GDPR notification and a loss of clients (consequence).” Written this way, the risk points directly to its controls and its owner.

Likelihood and impact are scored on scales agreed in advance, so that two people give the same score to the same risk. Four levels avoid the comfortable middle choice of a five-level scale. Likelihood is described in frequency or probability over a period: 1 = rare (less than once in 10 years), 2 = unlikely (once in 3 to 10 years), 3 = possible (once in 1 to 3 years), 4 = likely (once a year or more).

Impact is described in several dimensions, and the highest one wins: financial (loss in euros, as a share of revenue), operational (how long a critical activity stops), legal and regulatory (fines, notification, sanctions), reputation (local complaint up to national press) and people (harm to customers or staff). Example: 4 = more than 2 % of revenue, or activity stopped more than one week, or a regulator’s sanction, or national press coverage.

The risk score is often likelihood × impact, giving 1 to 16 on a 4 × 4 scale, shown on a heat map with likelihood on one axis and impact on the other. Colours turn scores into decisions: for example 1-3 green (accept), 4-8 amber (treat if cost-effective, follow up), 9-16 red (treat as a priority, management informed). Be aware of the limits: a risk with impact 4 and likelihood 1 scores 4, the same as a frequent minor nuisance, yet it may deserve far more attention. Many organisations add a rule such as “any impact 4 is reviewed by management whatever the score”.

Calibrate scales with real numbers from the organisation: its revenue, its critical processes, its past incidents. Scales copied from another company give scores that mean nothing to the people who must decide.
points: Risk statement: cause → event → consequence, so it points to controls and an owner.
Four-level scales avoid the middle choice; define each level in words and numbers.
Impact dimensions: financial, operational, legal, reputation, people; the highest wins.
Score = likelihood × impact on a heat map, with colours tied to decisions.
Watch high-impact, low-likelihood risks: add a rule so they are not hidden by a low score.

example.code:
Impact  4 |   4    8   12   16
        3 |   3    6    9   12
        2 |   2    4    6    8
        1 |   1    2    3    4
          +--------------------
              1    2    3    4   Likelihood

 1-3 green: accept and monitor   4-8 amber: treat if worthwhile   9-16 red: treat now
example.note: A 4 × 4 heat map. Each cell is likelihood × impact; the colour bands are the decision rules agreed with management.

lessons.title: Running an assessment: ISO 27005 in practice
text: ISO 27005:2022 describes two ways to identify information security risks. The asset-based approach starts from the asset inventory: for each important asset, list the threats and vulnerabilities that apply. It is thorough and fits ISO 27001, but can produce long, repetitive lists. The event-based (scenario) approach starts from the events that would hurt the organisation, such as ransomware, fraud or a supplier outage, and works out how they could happen. It produces fewer, more meaningful risks. Many teams combine them.

The information comes from people and from data. Run workshops with the business owners and IT, one process or one system at a time, with prepared questions. Use existing sources: past incidents and near-misses, audit findings, vulnerability scan and penetration test results, threat intelligence for your sector (for example ANSSI’s threat reports for France), and the obligations of laws and contracts.

In the workshop, keep the discussion concrete. Ask what happened before, what would worry them most, what they could not work without, and what is done today to prevent it. Score likelihood and impact with the agreed scales on the screen, note the reasons for each score, and identify the existing controls. When people disagree on a score, write down both views and the reason, then decide with the risk owner.

After the workshops, the GRC analyst consolidates: removes duplicates, checks the scores are consistent across workshops (the same ransomware risk should not be 4 in one and 12 in another), ranks the risks and prepares the treatment proposals. The result is validated with the risk owners, then presented to management with the top risks and the decisions needed.

A first full assessment of a mid-sized company often takes several weeks. Afterwards, it is updated: once a year in full, and whenever something important changes, such as a new system, a merger, a major incident or a new law. A register that is not updated becomes a document nobody trusts.
points: Asset-based (from the inventory) or event-based (from scenarios); often combined.
Sources: workshops, incidents, audit findings, scans and pentests, threat intelligence, legal obligations.
In workshops: concrete questions, agreed scales on screen, reasons written for each score.
Consolidate: remove duplicates, align scores across workshops, rank, validate with owners.
Full update yearly and after major change; an outdated register loses all credibility.

example.code:
Workshop: payroll process            Participants: HR director, payroll lead, IT
Questions
  1. Which incidents or near-misses in the last 3 years?
  2. What would stop payroll from being paid on time?
  3. Who can change an employee's bank details, and how is it checked?
  4. Which suppliers are involved (payroll software, bank)?
  5. What would hurt most: late pay, wrong pay or leaked salaries?
Output: 6 risks scored, 9 existing controls, 2 disagreements to settle with the HR director
example.note: A workshop plan for one process: concrete questions lead to concrete, well-scored risks.

lessons.title: EBIOS Risk Manager, the French method
text: EBIOS Risk Manager (EBIOS RM) is the risk method published by ANSSI, the French national cybersecurity agency, in 2018. It is widely used in France, especially in the public sector, operators of vital importance and organisations affected by NIS2, and it appears in many French GRC job offers. It is event-based: it starts from what the organisation must protect and from who would want to attack it.

The method has five workshops. Workshop 1, scope and security baseline: define the business values (essential missions and information), the supporting assets, the feared events and their severity, and check the baseline of rules already applied, such as the ANSSI hygiene guide or ISO 27001. Workshop 2, risk origins: identify who could attack (cybercriminals, competitors, hacktivists, states, insiders) and what they would aim for, and keep the most relevant pairs of risk origin and target objective.

Workshop 3, strategic scenarios: describe how an attacker would reach the business values at a high level, often through the ecosystem: suppliers, partners, service providers with access. This workshop maps the third parties and their level of threat. Workshop 4, operational scenarios: detail the technical steps of the most important strategic scenarios (initial access, spreading, exploitation) and assess their likelihood. Workshop 5, risk treatment: summarise the risks, define the security measures and the continuous improvement plan, and present the residual risks.

Compared with a classic asset-based approach, EBIOS RM produces fewer but more realistic scenarios, takes the supply chain into account, and speaks the language of business values that management understands. It takes more time and needs experienced facilitators, so smaller organisations often use a light version, keeping workshops 1, 3 and 5.

Other methods you may meet: NIST SP 800-30 in American contexts, and MEHARI, an older French method. In an interview, it is enough to explain the five EBIOS RM workshops, why the ecosystem matters, and how you would adapt the method to the size of the organisation.
points: EBIOS RM: ANSSI’s method (2018), common in French public bodies, critical operators and NIS2 entities.
W1 scope and security baseline; W2 risk origins and target objectives; W3 strategic scenarios via the ecosystem.
W4 operational scenarios (technical attack steps, likelihood); W5 risk treatment and improvement plan.
Strengths: business values, realistic scenarios, supply chain; cost: time and skilled facilitation.
Also met: NIST SP 800-30 (US), MEHARI (older French method).

example.code:
Business value      Patient records of a private clinic
Feared event        Records published online (severity 4)
Risk origin         Cybercriminal group -> target: extortion
Strategic scenario  Group compromises the clinic's IT service provider,
                    then uses its remote access to reach the records server
Operational steps   Phishing of a provider technician -> remote access tool
                    -> admin rights -> data exfiltration -> ransom demand
Measures            MFA for provider access, access only on request, logging and alerts,
                    contract clauses on the provider's security
example.note: An EBIOS RM chain from workshop 1 to 5: the attack goes through a supplier, which a pure asset list would likely miss.

lessons.title: Putting a number on risk
text: Qualitative scores help to rank risks, but management often asks “how much could it cost, and is the control worth the money?”. Quantitative analysis answers in currency. The classic formulas come from insurance. The single loss expectancy (SLE) is the cost of one occurrence: asset value × exposure factor, the share of the value lost. The annualised rate of occurrence (ARO) is how many times a year the event is expected: 0.2 means once in five years. The annualised loss expectancy is ALE = SLE × ARO.

Example: a ransomware attack on the online shop would cost about 400,000 euros (lost sales, recovery, experts, penalties): that is the SLE. Based on the sector and the company’s exposure, it is estimated at once every four years, so ARO = 0.25. ALE = 400,000 × 0.25 = 100,000 euros a year. If offline backups and an endpoint detection tool cost 30,000 euros a year and bring the ARO down to 0.1 and the SLE to 150,000 (faster recovery), the new ALE is 15,000. The control reduces expected loss by 85,000 a year for 30,000: it is worth it.

This comparison is called the return on security investment: (reduction in ALE − cost of the control) / cost of the control, here (85,000 − 30,000) / 30,000 ≈ 1.8. It is a strong argument in a budget meeting, as long as you explain the assumptions behind the numbers.

Numbers in cyber risk are uncertain. Good practice is to use ranges and sources rather than single precise values: a minimum, a most likely value and a maximum for the loss, based on the company’s own data, insurance figures and published studies. FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) is a recognised model that breaks risk into loss event frequency and loss magnitude, and uses ranges and simulations. It is popular in large companies and with cyber insurers.

Quantify the few risks where a decision depends on it, typically the top risks and large investments; keep qualitative scores for the rest. Always show your assumptions, so that people can challenge them, and update the figures after an incident or when the business changes.
points: SLE = asset value × exposure factor (cost of one occurrence).
ARO = expected occurrences per year (0.25 = once in four years).
ALE = SLE × ARO; compare the ALE before and after a control with the control’s yearly cost.
Return on security investment = (ALE reduction − control cost) / control cost.
Use ranges and state assumptions; FAIR models frequency and magnitude with ranges.

example.code:
Before control      After control
SLE (one attack)         400,000 EUR         150,000 EUR
ARO (per year)           0.25                0.10
ALE = SLE x ARO          100,000 EUR         15,000 EUR
Control cost per year                        30,000 EUR
ALE reduction                                85,000 EUR
Return on investment     (85,000 - 30,000) / 30,000 = 1.83
example.note: Offline backups and endpoint detection reduce both the frequency and the cost of a ransomware attack.

lessons.title: Treating risks and keeping the register
text: There are four ways to treat a risk, with names that vary between standards. Reduce (modify, mitigate): add or improve controls to lower likelihood or impact, the most common choice. Transfer (share): move part of the financial impact to someone else, through cyber insurance or a contract with a supplier; the responsibility towards customers and regulators stays with you. Avoid: stop the activity that creates the risk, for example decide not to store card numbers at all. Accept (retain): keep the risk as it is, because it is within appetite or because treating it would cost more than it saves.

Acceptance must be a decision, not a default. It is made by the risk owner at the right level of authority, in writing, with the reason and a review date. A high risk accepted by a junior employee, or a risk that nobody ever looked at, is not accepted: it is ignored.

Each treatment becomes an action plan: the actions, an owner for each, a budget, a deadline, and the expected residual risk after completion. The GRC analyst follows the actions, raises those that are late, and updates the residual score when an action is finished and its control works. A plan of 80 actions with no priorities is a common mistake; focus on the actions that reduce the top risks most.

The risk register is the central tool. For each risk: an identifier, the statement, the category, the asset or process, the owner, the existing controls, inherent likelihood, impact and score, residual likelihood, impact and score, the treatment decision, the action plan and its status, key risk indicators, and the dates of the last review and the next one. It can be a spreadsheet or a GRC tool, but it must be the single, up-to-date source.

Reviews keep it alive: risk owners review their risks at least quarterly for the top risks and yearly for the rest, scores are updated after incidents and audit findings, and changes are reported to the security committee. Key risk indicators linked to the top risks show between reviews whether a risk is getting worse.
points: Reduce, transfer (insurance, contract), avoid (stop the activity), accept (decision within appetite).
Acceptance: by the risk owner, in writing, with a reason and a review date.
Action plan: actions, owners, budget, deadlines, expected residual risk; focus on the top risks.
Register: statement, owner, controls, inherent and residual scores, treatment, actions, KRIs, review dates.
Review top risks quarterly, all risks yearly, and after incidents or audit findings.

example.code:
ID    Risk (cause -> event -> consequence)                   Owner    Inh.  Treatment  Res.  Next review
R-03  Passwords only on remote access -> account takeover   CIO      12    Reduce     4     30 Sep
      -> customer data theft, GDPR notification                       (MFA by 31 Jul)
R-07  Single payroll supplier -> outage at month end         HR dir   8     Transfer   6     31 Dec
      -> late salaries                                                 (contract SLA, penalties)
R-11  Card numbers stored for refunds -> theft -> PCI fines  CFO      12    Avoid      1     31 Dec
                                                                       (tokenisation)
example.note: Three register lines, three different treatments; each has an owner, a residual target and a review date.

lessons.title: Suppliers and business continuity
text: Many incidents come through suppliers: a software provider with remote access, a cloud service holding customer data, a payroll company. Third-party risk management starts with an inventory of suppliers and a tiering: critical suppliers (access to sensitive data or systems, or essential to a critical process) get a full assessment, others a lighter one. NIS2 asks entities to manage supply chain security, and DORA asks financial entities to keep a register of all their ICT contracts and to supervise critical providers closely.

The assessment combines a security questionnaire, the supplier’s certifications and reports (ISO 27001 certificate and its scope, SOC 2 type II report and its exceptions), public information, and for the most critical ones an audit or a call with their security team. The result is a risk rating and conditions. The contract then carries the requirements: security obligations, notification of incidents within a set time, right to audit, data location, subcontracting rules, return or destruction of data at the end, and an exit plan.

Business continuity prepares the organisation to keep its critical activities running during a disruption. It starts with a business impact analysis (BIA): for each process, what happens over time if it stops, which systems, people and suppliers it needs, and how long it can be down. The BIA sets the recovery objectives that IT must meet.

Three numbers matter. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum time to restore a process or system after a disruption, for example 4 hours for the online shop. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum data loss acceptable, expressed in time: an RPO of 1 hour means backups or replication at least every hour. The maximum tolerable period of disruption (MTPD) is the point beyond which the damage becomes unacceptable; the RTO must be shorter.

The business continuity plan (BCP) describes how the business keeps working: workarounds, alternative sites, crisis team and communication. The disaster recovery plan (DRP, PRA in French) describes how IT restores systems. Plans are useless without tests: tabletop exercises with the crisis team, restore tests, and failover tests for the most critical systems, with lessons learned recorded and actions followed.
points: Tier suppliers; assess critical ones deeply (questionnaire, ISO 27001 scope, SOC 2 type II exceptions).
Contract clauses: security duties, incident notification, right to audit, data location, subcontracting, exit.
BIA: impact over time, dependencies and how long each process can stop.
RTO: time to restore; RPO: acceptable data loss; MTPD: point of unacceptable damage (RTO < MTPD).
BCP (business keeps working) and DRP (IT restores); test them and follow the lessons learned.

example.code:
Process           MTPD      RTO      RPO      Key dependencies
Online orders     24 h      4 h      15 min   Shop platform, payment provider, stock DB
Customer support  3 days    24 h     4 h      Ticket tool (SaaS), phone provider
Payroll           5 days    48 h     24 h     Payroll supplier, bank file transfer
Accounting close  10 days   5 days   24 h     ERP, file server
example.note: Extract of a business impact analysis: each RTO is shorter than the MTPD, and the RPO drives the backup frequency.

items: Context → identify → analyse → evaluate → treat, with monitoring and communication
Level of risk before (or without) controls
Level of risk with the controls in place
Manager with the authority and budget to decide the treatment
What we accept overall / limits per area / what we could survive
Defined in frequency, for example 1 = less than once in 10 years
Financial, operational, legal, reputation, people; the highest wins
Likelihood × impact grid with colours tied to decisions
ANSSI method in five workshops, from business values to treatment
Asset value × exposure factor: cost of one occurrence
Expected occurrences per year (0.25 = once in four years)
SLE × ARO: expected loss per year
Model of loss frequency and magnitude, using ranges
Share the financial impact: insurance, contract
Stop the activity that creates the risk
Written decision by the risk owner, with a reason and a review date
Single, up-to-date list of risks, scores, owners, treatments and actions
Critical suppliers get a full assessment, others a lighter one
Business impact analysis: impact over time, dependencies, tolerable downtime
Maximum time to restore a process or system
Maximum acceptable data loss, in time
Maximum tolerable period of disruption; RTO must be shorter

pitfalls: Writing topics instead of risks (“cyber attack”, “GDPR”): use cause, event and consequence.
Letting each workshop score with its own feelings: agree the scales first and align scores afterwards.
Hiding rare but catastrophic risks behind a low likelihood × impact score.
Calling it acceptance when nobody with authority decided: acceptance is a written decision.
Presenting precise money figures without their assumptions: use ranges and sources.
Assessing suppliers once at signature and never again.
Writing a continuity plan that has never been tested.

exercises.q: Put the steps of the ISO 31000 / ISO 27005 risk process in order.
steps: Establish the context and the criteria
Evaluate against the acceptance criteria and rank
exercises.answer: Context first, because the scales and criteria must exist before anyone scores. Assessment has three steps (identify, analyse, evaluate), then treatment, then monitoring, which starts the cycle again. Communication with stakeholders runs through all steps.

exercises.q: Match each treatment option with an example.
pairs: Deploy MFA on all remote access
Stop storing card numbers and use a payment provider’s tokens
The risk owner signs off a low residual risk until next year’s review
exercises.answer: Reducing changes likelihood or impact, transferring moves part of the financial impact, avoiding removes the activity, and accepting is a recorded decision to keep the risk. Note that transfer never moves the responsibility towards customers or regulators.

exercises.q: Which risk statement is written well enough to be assessed?
options: Because supplier bank details can be changed by one person without a call-back, a fraudster could redirect payments, causing a loss of up to 200,000 euros
IT security is not good enough
exercises.answer: The third statement has a cause (one person can change bank details without verification), an event (a fraudster redirects payments) and a consequence (a loss of up to 200,000 euros). It points directly to the controls: a second approver and a call-back on a known number. The others are topics or opinions.

exercises.q: In B4, compute the risk score as likelihood × impact.
exercises.explain: 3 × 4 = 12 out of 16, in the red band of a typical heat map (9 to 16): the risk must be treated as a priority and management informed.

exercises.q: In B5, compute the annualised loss expectancy (ALE) from the asset value, the exposure factor and the ARO.
exercises.explain: SLE = 500,000 × 0.6 = 300,000 euros for one occurrence; ALE = SLE × ARO = 300,000 × 0.2 = 60,000 euros a year. A control costing less than the reduction it brings to this figure is worth considering.

exercises.q: In D2, compute the return on security investment: (ALE before − ALE after − control cost) / control cost.
exercises.explain: The control reduces the expected loss by 60,000 a year and costs 25,000, so the return is (60,000 − 25,000) / 25,000 = 1.4: each euro spent saves 1.4 euros on top of its cost. Present the assumptions behind the two ALEs with the result.

groups.name: Time to restore
items: RTO of 4 hours for the online shop

groups.name: Limit of tolerable damage
items: MTPD of 24 hours for online orders
After 5 days without payroll, staff leave

exercises.answer: The RTO is how fast a process or system must be back, the RPO how much data (in time) can be lost, which drives backup or replication frequency, and the MTPD is the point after which the damage becomes unacceptable. The RTO must always be shorter than the MTPD.

exercises.q: A business team wants to sign with a new cloud payroll provider that will hold all salary and bank data. Walk through the supplier review.

choices.label: Classify the supplier as critical (sensitive data, essential process) and plan a full assessment
choices.feedback: Right: tiering decides how deep the review goes, and this supplier holds sensitive data for an essential process.

choices.label: Send the same short questionnaire as for every supplier
choices.feedback: A light review for a critical supplier misses what matters: tier first, then adapt the depth.

choices.label: Refuse, because cloud payroll is too risky
choices.feedback: GRC helps the business go ahead safely; refusing without assessment is not a risk-based decision.

steps.text: The supplier sends an ISO 27001 certificate. What do you check?

choices.label: That the certificate’s scope covers the payroll service and the data centres used, and that it is still valid
choices.feedback: Yes: a certificate only covers its scope; it may cover the head office but not the service you buy.

choices.label: Nothing more: a certificate proves the supplier is secure
choices.feedback: A certificate shows a management system exists for a given scope; it does not cover everything or replace your own questions.

choices.label: Ask for their full list of passwords
choices.feedback: Never: you ask for evidence of controls, not for secrets.

steps.text: The assessment is mostly positive, but data is hosted outside the EU and incident notification is not in the contract. What do you recommend?

choices.label: Go ahead with conditions: EU hosting option or valid transfer safeguards, a 24-hour incident notification clause, right to audit and an exit plan, then residual risk accepted by the HR director
choices.feedback: Right: conditions turn the findings into contract terms, and the business owner accepts what remains.

choices.label: Approve as is, since the questionnaire was mostly positive
choices.feedback: The two gaps are real (GDPR transfers, incident notification) and are easy to fix in the contract before signing.

choices.label: Block the project until the supplier moves all its data centres
choices.feedback: Too strong: safeguards and an EU option can solve the transfer issue without stopping the project.

exercises.answer: Tier the supplier, assess it in proportion (questionnaire, certificate scope, SOC 2 exceptions, transfers), turn the gaps into contract conditions, and have the business owner accept the residual risk in writing.

exercises.q: What is the name of the French national cybersecurity agency’s risk method, organised in five workshops? Answer with its usual short name.
exercises.answer: EBIOS Risk Manager (EBIOS RM), published by ANSSI: scope and security baseline, risk origins, strategic scenarios through the ecosystem, operational scenarios, and risk treatment.

exercises.q: Write a likelihood scale and an impact scale (4 levels each) for a 200-person online retailer with 40 million euros of revenue.
exercises.hint: Frequencies for likelihood; several dimensions with numbers for impact.
exercises.answer: Likelihood: 1 rare (less than once in 10 years), 2 unlikely (once in 3 to 10 years), 3 possible (once in 1 to 3 years), 4 likely (once a year or more). Impact, the highest dimension wins: 1 minor (loss under 40,000 euros, shop slowed less than 1 hour, no legal effect, a few customer complaints); 2 moderate (40,000 to 200,000 euros, shop down less than 4 hours, internal GDPR incident without notification, local social media noise); 3 serious (200,000 to 800,000 euros, shop down 4 to 24 hours, CNIL notification, national online press); 4 critical (over 800,000 euros, that is 2 % of revenue, shop down more than 24 hours, sanction by a regulator or notification of all customers, national TV or long-lasting damage to the brand). The thresholds are tied to the company’s own revenue and its peak-day sales.

exercises.q: Your risk register has 140 risks, 90 actions, and management says it does not read it. What do you change?
exercises.answer: I keep the full register as the working tool, but I change what reaches management. I merge duplicates and risks that are really the same scenario, which often reduces the list by a third. I rank by residual score and select the top 10 risks, each with one sentence, its owner, its trend and the main action. I check that every top risk has an action plan with a date and drop or postpone low-value actions. I add three to five key risk indicators tied to the top risks. Then I present a one-page summary at each security committee, with the decisions needed, and review the top risks with their owners every quarter.

exercises.q: The CFO asks whether the company should spend 120,000 euros a year on a managed detection and response service. How do you build the answer?
exercises.answer: I identify the risks the service addresses, mainly ransomware and data theft, and estimate their current ALE with ranges: the cost of one major incident (downtime, recovery, experts, notification, lost customers) and its yearly frequency, using our incidents, the sector’s data and insurer figures. I estimate the ALE with the service, which mainly reduces the impact through faster detection, and sometimes the frequency. I compare the reduction with the 120,000 euros, show the return on investment and the assumptions, add what numbers do not capture (NIS2 or client requirements, insurance conditions, the team’s capacity at night), and present two or three options, for example the service, a cheaper partial option and doing nothing, with the residual risk of each so that the CFO can decide.

interview.q: What is the difference between inherent and residual risk?
interview.a: Inherent risk is the level of risk before taking the existing controls into account. Residual risk is the level that remains with the controls in place. The gap shows how much the controls bring, and residual risk is what management compares with its appetite: it either accepts it or asks for further treatment.

interview.q: What are the four ways to treat a risk?
interview.a: Reduce it with controls, transfer part of the financial impact through insurance or contracts, avoid it by stopping the activity that creates it, or accept it within the appetite. Acceptance is a written decision by the risk owner with a reason and a review date, not the absence of a decision. In practice most risks get a mix, for example reduce with MFA and transfer the remaining financial impact to an insurer.

interview.q: How do you make sure two workshops score risks consistently?
interview.a: By agreeing the scales before any workshop, with definitions in words and numbers for each level, and showing them during the session. I write the reason for each score, then compare the scores across workshops during consolidation: the same scenario should not get very different scores without an explanation. Disagreements are settled with the risk owner, and I calibrate the scales with the company’s real data such as revenue and past incidents.

interview.q: Explain SLE, ARO and ALE with an example.
interview.a: SLE is the cost of one occurrence: asset value times the exposure factor. ARO is how many times a year we expect it. ALE is SLE times ARO. If a data breach would cost 300,000 euros and we expect it once every five years, the ALE is 60,000 euros a year. If a control costs 20,000 a year and halves the frequency, it saves 30,000 a year, so it pays for itself. I always give ranges and assumptions with such numbers.

It is the risk method of ANSSI, the French cybersecurity agency, used widely in France. It has five workshops: scope and security baseline, risk origins and their objectives, strategic scenarios that go through the ecosystem of suppliers and partners, operational scenarios that detail the attack steps, and risk treatment. Its strengths are that it starts from business values and takes the supply chain into account, so its scenarios are realistic and easy to explain to management.

interview.q: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
interview.a: The RTO, recovery time objective, is how long a process or system can take to be restored after a disruption. The RPO, recovery point objective, is how much data, measured in time, we can afford to lose, so it drives the backup or replication frequency. Both come from the business impact analysis, and the RTO must be shorter than the maximum tolerable period of disruption.

interview.q: How do you assess a critical supplier?
interview.a: I tier suppliers first, then for a critical one I combine a security questionnaire, its certifications and reports, checking the scope of the ISO 27001 certificate and the exceptions in the SOC 2 type II report, data location and transfers, incident history and, if needed, a call with its security team or an audit. The findings become contract clauses: security obligations, incident notification within a set time, right to audit, subcontracting rules and an exit plan. The business owner accepts the residual risk, and the review is repeated every year or on any major change.
